anomaly_def.Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Execution-plan costing relies on stale, missing, or inaccurate catalog statistics, producing systematic cardinality misestimates and sub-optimal plans.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas, causing allocation failures and blocking new work.

When both root causes strike concurrently, the workload exhibits a mix of logical and infrastructural pathologies: queries choose wrong join orders or degrees of parallelism and then abruptly abort with system-level errors such as “cannot create shared memory segment,” “too many open files,” or “failed to start worker.” Batch jobs may swing between severe under-estimation (tiny memory grants leading to spills) and over-estimation (requests for memory or workers that the OS refuses), resulting in thrashing, frequent plan recompilations, intermittent session failures, and oscillating performance. Because failures appear in both the execution plan (row-count gaps, excessive I/O, temp spills) and the system log (resource exhaustion messages), symptoms can seem unrelated, elongating triage time.

Causal interplay: stale statistics can inflate optimizer estimates, prompting the engine to ask the OS for large memory areas, high parallel-worker counts, extra temp files, or additional file handles; if kernel quotas are tight, those requests are denied, turning a performance issue into hard errors and session drops. Conversely, once OS limits are hit, automatic statistics jobs and parallel scan workers cannot start, preventing statistics refreshes and locking the system into an ever more outdated cost model. This feedback loop escalates misestimation and resource starvation, degrading throughput and reliability across both transactional and analytical workloads.

entry.official_definition: Aborts any statement that waits longer than the specified amount of time while attempting to acquire a lock.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_timeout for a table, index, row, or other database object lock.
entry.workload_impact: The statement attempting to acquire the lock is aborted.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
